title: Project: Spotify Audio Features and Popularity
text:
For this project, I used the Spotify Tracks Dataset from Kaggle. This dataset has information on thousands of songs available on Spotify, including how popular each song is and various audio characteristics that describe how the song sounds and feels.
Each row in the dataset is one song. Here are the main variables I worked with:

track_name: The name of the song
artists: Who performed the song
popularity: A number from 0 to 100 showing how popular the song is on Spotify
danceability: How easy it is to dance to the song (0 = not danceable, 1 = very danceable)
energy: How intense or active the song feels (0 = calm, 1 = very energetic)
valence: How positive or happy the song sounds (0 = sad, 1 = happy)
tempo: How fast the song is, measured in beats per minute
track_genre: The genre the song belongs to

The main question I wanted to answer was: Do certain audio features like energy or danceability make a song more popular on Spotify?

title: Project: Spotify Audio Features and Popularity
text:
Data Cleaning

library(tidyverse)
library(here)


# Load the raw Spotify dataset using the here package
spotify_raw <- read_csv(here("data", "dataset.csv"))


# Step 1: SELECT only the columns we need
# This removes unneeded columns like IDs and keys
spotify_clean <- spotify_raw |>
  select(
    track_name,
    artists,
    track_genre,
    popularity,
    danceability,
    energy,
    valence,
    tempo
  )

# Step 2: FILTER out missing values and songs with zero popularity
# Songs with 0 popularity are usually unlisted or unreleased
spotify_clean <- spotify_clean |>
  filter(
    !is.na(popularity),
    !is.na(danceability),
    !is.na(energy),
    !is.na(valence),
    !is.na(tempo),
    popularity > 0
  )

# Step 3: MUTATE to group songs into popularity tiers
# Low = 0-33, Medium = 34-66, High = 67-100
spotify_clean <- spotify_clean |>
  mutate(
    popularity_tier = case_when(
      popularity < 34                    ~ "Low",
      popularity >= 34 & popularity < 67 ~ "Medium",
      popularity >= 67                   ~ "High"
    ),
    popularity_tier = factor(
      popularity_tier,
      levels = c("Low", "Medium", "High")
    )
  )

# Step 4: MUTATE to group songs by energy level
# Makes it easier to compare high vs low energy songs
spotify_clean <- spotify_clean |>
  mutate(
    energy_category = case_when(
      energy < 0.33  ~ "Low Energy",
      energy < 0.66  ~ "Medium Energy",
      energy >= 0.66 ~ "High Energy"
    ),
    energy_category = factor(
      energy_category,
      levels = c("Low Energy", "Medium Energy", "High Energy")
    )
  )

# Step 5: DISTINCT to remove duplicate songs
# Keeps only one entry per song and artist combination
spotify_clean <- spotify_clean |>
  distinct(track_name, artists, .keep_all = TRUE)

# Step 6: SUMMARIZE average popularity by genre
# This helps us see which genres perform best overall
genre_summary <- spotify_clean |>
  group_by(track_genre) |>
  summarize(
    avg_popularity = mean(popularity, na.rm = TRUE),
    count = n()
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(avg_popularity))

# Save the cleaned dataset
write_csv(spotify_clean, here("data", "spotify_clean.csv"))

To prepare the data for analysis, I went through several cleaning steps. First, I kept only the columns that were relevant to my questions and removed everything else. Then I filtered out any songs that had missing values or a popularity score of zero, since those songs are usually not publicly available on Spotify and would throw off my results. I also created two new grouping columns — one that places each song into a Low, Medium, or High popularity group, and another that groups songs by how energetic they are. After that, I removed any duplicate songs so that each track only appears once. Finally, I calculated the average popularity for each genre so I could compare them later.

title: Project: Spotify Audio Features and Popularity
text:
Visualization 1
This chart shows the average popularity of songs grouped by their energy level — Low, Medium, or High. The bars make it easy to compare whether more energetic songs tend to be more popular on Spotify. The small lines on top of each bar show how much variation exists within each group.

spotify_clean |>
  group_by(energy_category) |>
  summarize(
    avg_pop = mean(popularity, na.rm = TRUE),
    se_pop  = sd(popularity, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n())
  ) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x    = energy_category,
      y    = avg_pop,
      fill = energy_category
    )
  ) +
  geom_col(width = 0.55) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(ymin = avg_pop - se_pop, ymax = avg_pop + se_pop),
    width = 0.15,
    color = "gray30"
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = round(avg_pop, 1)),
    vjust    = -1.4,
    size     = 4.5,
    fontface = "bold",
    color    = "gray20"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Low Energy"    = "#E07B54",
      "Medium Energy" = "#5B8DB8",
      "High Energy"   = "#4CAF78"
    )
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 60),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Does Energy Level Affect Song Popularity?",
    subtitle = "Average Spotify popularity score for each energy group",
    x        = "Energy Level",
    y        = "Average Popularity Score",
    caption  = "Source: Spotify Tracks Dataset, Kaggle"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.title         = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle      = element_text(color = "gray40"),
    legend.position    = "none",
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor   = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x        = element_text(size = 12)
  )







Figure 1: Bar chart comparing average Spotify popularity scores across three energy level groups.

title: Project: Spotify Audio Features and Popularity
text:
Visualization 2
This boxplot looks at how popularity scores are spread out within each energy group, broken up further by popularity tier (Low, Medium, High). Unlike the bar chart above which shows averages, a boxplot shows the full range — the middle values, the spread, and any outliers. This gives a more complete picture of how energy relates to popularity across different tiers.

spotify_clean |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x    = energy_category,
      y    = popularity,
      fill = energy_category
    )
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(
    outlier.alpha = 0.2,
    outlier.size  = 0.8,
    width         = 0.6
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~popularity_tier, labeller = label_both) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Low Energy"    = "#E07B54",
      "Medium Energy" = "#5B8DB8",
      "High Energy"   = "#4CAF78"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "How Does Energy Level Relate to Popularity Tier?",
    subtitle = "Popularity score distributions for Low, Medium, and High energy songs",
    x        = "Energy Category",
    y        = "Popularity Score (0–100)",
    fill     = "Energy Level",
    caption  = "Source: Spotify Tracks Dataset, Kaggle"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.title       = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle    = element_text(color = "gray40"),
    legend.position  = "none",
    axis.text.x      = element_text(angle = 15, hjust = 1),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    strip.text       = element_text(face = "bold")
  )







Figure 2: Boxplot comparing popularity score distributions across energy categories, grouped by popularity tier.

title: Project: Spotify Audio Features and Popularity
text:
Visualization 3
This horizontal bar chart shows the top 10 music genres by average popularity on Spotify. Each bar represents one genre, sorted from most to least popular. This gives a clear view of which types of music tend to perform best on the platform.

genre_summary |>
  slice_max(avg_popularity, n = 10) |>
  mutate(
    track_genre = fct_reorder(track_genre, avg_popularity)
  ) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x    = avg_popularity,
      y    = track_genre,
      fill = avg_popularity
    )
  ) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = round(avg_popularity, 1)),
    hjust = -0.2,
    size  = 3.5,
    color = "gray20"
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#5B8DB8", high = "#1a3a5c") +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
  labs(
    title    = "Which Spotify Genres Are the Most Popular?",
    subtitle = "Top 10 genres by average popularity score",
    x        = "Average Popularity Score (0–100)",
    y        = "Genre",
    caption  = "Source: Spotify Tracks Dataset, Kaggle"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.title         = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle      = element_text(color = "gray40"),
    legend.position    = "none",
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor   = element_blank()
  )







Figure 3: Bar chart of the top 10 Spotify genres ranked by average popularity score.
